caption:
Your Pi extensions break when Pi changes.
A system on your Mac repairs them.

Three times a day,
it checks for a new Pi release.

An Opus agent fixes.
An Astra agent, from another vendor, reviews.

In the old design, the fixer
saw every extension at once.

But each review and repair
saw only one.

So a question about two extensions could not
be repaired. It got stuck, three reviews in a row.

The new design gives both sides
the same scope.

Now there are two trees:
one that fixes, and one that reviews.

The main fixer owns the whole job.
It never touches code.

It forks one delegate per extension.
Each delegate owns one patch, in one clone.

The review tree is a mirror: a main reviewer,
and one reviewer delegate per extension.

The system makes every fork
and carries every message. It never judges.

Delegates never talk to each other. Only the
two main agents see across extensions.
Here is one round.

First, the quota gate. If there is not
enough quota left, the round waits.

Then each clone moves to
the newest main on GitHub.

The fixer delegates work in parallel. Each one
sends its diff straight to its reviewer.

Each reviewer delegate answers:
approve, or revise.

The main reviewer reads all verdicts together. It can
reject a fix that breaks another extension.

Then the main fixer:
the last gate before anything leaves.

For each extension, it releases,
holds back, or sends the findings back.

It can also change a finding.
The reviewer sees the reason next round.

A released fix gets an ntfy notice, then a push.
A product change also waits for your tap.

Nothing moves while a main agent decides.
So nothing races.

One rule holds this together: the main agents
can only narrow what gets published.

They can hold an approval back. They can never
release what a reviewer rejected.
Each delegate pair gets three reviews.

If its work is released,
the pair is done. No handoff.

If three reviews pass without a release, each one
writes a handoff, and a fresh pair continues.

Every run starts fresh main agents. The old fixer
once grew to 726,000 tokens in three days.

Work carries over in the clones,
the handoffs, and the open questions.

Questions reach you on Telegram,
one at a time.

Your answer wakes the current
main fixer, at any hour.

It passes the answer to the delegate that asked.
If it retired, a fresh one gets the context note.

The next question goes out only after your answer
is handled. Questions it settled disappear first.

When one concern touches two extensions,
the main fixer asks you once, about the decision.

The first test is Pi 1.4.0. It fixes the bug
that two unpublished patches worked around.

To pass, the system drops both patches, and asks
you before it removes pi-simple-team's workaround.

The design is not built yet.
It waits for your go-ahead.
